analysis.one_liner: Charges hardrock miners a 12.5% royalty on federal land and funds cleanup of abandoned mines.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House Natural Resources subcommittee after being referred there on June 27, 2013, with only two cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 1872 mining law, companies can take gold, silver, copper and other hardrock minerals from federal land without paying any royalty, buy the land cheaply, and leave cleanup of old mines to taxpayers. This bill would charge miners 12.5% of their gross income as a royalty, require annual claim fees, stop issuing new land patents, tighten permits and cleanup bonds, and impose a small per-ton fee to pay for cleaning up abandoned mines. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently absorb the cost of cleaning up tens of thousands of abandoned hardrock mines and receive nothing when companies extract minerals from public land; the bill directs royalties to deficit reduction and per-ton fees to an Abandoned Mine Cleanup Fund for grants to restore contaminated land and water [S2] [S3]. Communities near abandoned mines and Western water users also gain, since the bill funds reclamation of land and water damaged by past mining [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near abandoned mines

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 12.5% royalty on the gross income from production of locatable minerals on federal claims, deposited in the Treasury and used for deficit or debt reduction [S2] [S3].
Creates an Abandoned Mine Cleanup Fund from a 7-cents-per-ton fee on displaced mining material, used for grants to public entities to reclaim land and water damaged by past mining [S2].

Closes what reformers call the 1872 mining law's loopholes: annual $200 claim maintenance fees replace nominal work requirements, a $50 location fee applies to new claims, and no new patents are issued for claims whose applications were filed after September 30, 1994 [S2] [S3].

Requires exploration and operations permits, financial assurance bonds covering reclamation and water treatment, restoration of disturbed land, and lets states, local governments, and Indian tribes petition to withdraw federal land from mining to protect watersheds, wildlife, or cultural values [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies operating on federal land, who would pay the 12.5% royalty, annual claim fees, the per-ton reclamation fee, and the cost of permits, reclamation bonds, and cleanup performance [S2] [S3]. Some of those costs could be passed on in mineral prices, and the industry argues the royalty could reduce domestic mining and mining jobs [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Hardrock mining companies on federal land

drawbacks.text: A 12.5% royalty would raise the cost of producing gold, copper, and other metals from federal land; the industry argues this could shift production overseas and cost mining jobs, a cost an honest supporter should acknowledge (policy mechanism; industry burden is in the bill text) [S3].

The bill applies to claims located before enactment and to existing operations after a transition period, disrupting expectations built under the 1872 law and adding a permitting process that could delay projects on federal land [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would end a one-of-a-kind arrangement in which the government charges no royalty for hardrock minerals taken from public land while taxpayers cover abandoned-mine cleanup, so the main gains (royalty revenue for deficit reduction and a funded cleanup program) outweigh the added costs to miners. The main cost is borne by a specific industry, though some of it may reach consumers through mineral prices, and the added permitting could slow some projects.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2015 without a hearing, markup, or vote [S5] [S1].

narrative.text: Representative Edward Markey introduced the bill on June 20, 2013, joined by Representatives Rush Holt and Raúl Grijalva [S1] [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources on June 20, 2013, and on June 27, 2013, to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources [S5].
No further action was recorded through the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies, which kept extracting gold, silver, and copper from federal land without paying royalties, and continued to leave cleanup of abandoned mines to taxpayers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hardrock mining companies on public land

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and both cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill died in committee under a Republican majority without any recorded Republican support [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Hardrock mining (gold, silver, copper and other locatable minerals on federal land)
industries.note: The bill would charge the industry a 12.5% royalty for the first time, plus annual claim fees, a per-ton reclamation fee, and full-cost cleanup bonds. Its interest runs against the public's in this bill because its current advantage is paying nothing for public minerals while taxpayers absorb abandoned-mine cleanup costs.

The Abandoned Mine Cleanup Fund would pay grants to public entities for reclamation work, creating funded cleanup projects. That benefit runs alongside the public's interest in restored land and water.
